title: Georgia Democrats for Governor Clash on Key Issues in Latest Debate - NewsBreak
text:
By Archith Seshadri No media credit provided. ,
2 hours ago
ATLANTA, Ga. ( WRBL ) — Georgia voters are getting a clearer picture of the top Democratic contenders for governor after a wide-ranging debate tackling some of the state’s most pressing issues.
The candidates — Keisha Lance Bottoms, Geoff Duncan, and Michael Thurmond — addressed topics ranging from data centers and abortion to immigration and economic policy.
Shared Ground on Healthcare, Rural Hospitals
Despite their differences, all three candidates found common ground on several key issues — including expanding Medicaid and preventing rural hospital closures.
Bottoms pointed to her record as Atlanta’s mayor, highlighting investments in affordable housing, education, and small businesses. She also emphasized the need to expand workforce training programs to make Georgia more competitive.
“People are concerned about affordability in this state… access to health care… and opportunities for small businesses,” Bottoms said.
RELATED: Key points from Wednesday’s Democratic gubernatorial debate
Duncan, a former Republican lieutenant governor now running as a Democrat, said restoring trust in government and working across party lines would be central to his administration.
He outlined an ambitious first 100 days agenda, including passing gun legislation, repealing Georgia’s so-called “heartbeat bill,” expanding Medicaid, and investing in programs to address poverty — such as childcare and housing support.
Thurmond leaned on his experience as former labor commissioner and head of Georgia’s Division of Family and Children Services, stressing a results-driven approach.
He said one of his first actions would be to declare a statewide housing affordability crisis.
“Access to quality, affordable housing is not just an urban issue — it impacts communities across Georgia, especially in rural areas,” Thurmond said.
A recent Emerson College poll shows Bottoms with a slight lead at 35%, followed by Duncan at 11% and Thurmond at 7%. However, about 40% of voters remain undecided — leaving the race far from settled.
Across the board, voters say their top concerns are the economy, access to affordable healthcare, and rising housing costs.
The deadline to register for Georgia’s May 19 primary election is April 20.
If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the top two candidates will advance to a runoff election scheduled for June 16.
